config.title: Micro-Frontend Architecture

intro.title: Micro-Frontend Architecture
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a modular e-commerce application composed of multiple independent Angular micro-frontends that work together as a unified user experience. You'll learn the core concept of micro-frontend architecture, where large applications are broken down into smaller, independently deployable frontend modules that can be developed and maintained by separate teams. The lesson covers key technologies including Angular Elements for creating custom elements, Module Federation for runtime code sharing, and routing strategies for seamless navigation between micro-frontends. You'll implement a main shell application that dynamically loads product catalog, shopping cart, and user profile micro-frontends, each built as standalone Angular applications. By the end, you'll understand how to architect scalable frontend systems that promote team autonomy while maintaining consistent user experiences across different application domains.
intro.usecase: Micro-Frontend Architecture is essential in large-scale applications like e-commerce platforms where different teams manage product catalogs, shopping carts, user profiles, and payment systems as independent Angular applications that compose into one seamless user experience. Major platforms like Netflix use micro-frontends to allow separate teams to develop and deploy their search interface, content discovery panels, video players, and user settings independently while maintaining a unified dashboard. This architecture is particularly valuable in enterprise applications where HR portals, financial dashboards, inventory management, and reporting tools can be developed by different teams using different Angular versions, then integrated into a single application shell. Banking applications leverage micro-frontends to isolate account management, transaction history, loan applications, and investment portfolios as separate deployable units that share common navigation and branding components.

objectives: Configure multiple Angular applications to function as independent micro-frontends
Implement Module Federation to enable runtime sharing of components between applications
Construct a shell application that dynamically loads and renders micro-frontend modules
Integrate shared libraries and dependencies across micro-frontend boundaries
Apply routing strategies to navigate between different micro-frontend applications
Manipulate build configurations to support micro-frontend deployment architectures
Initialize communication channels between independent micro-frontend applications

steps.title: Import Angular core modules and create main AppComponent
steps.instruction: Import Component from '@angular/core' and create the main AppComponent class with basic structure.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator to define the component metadata, including its selector and template.

seedCode.App.tsx: // Import Component from '@angular/core' and create the AppComponent class

steps.expectedOutcome: You will have the foundational Angular component structure set up for building micro-frontend architecture.
successCriteria: Component is imported from '@angular/core' and the AppComponent class is created with @Component decorator, selector, and template.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've imported Component from '@angular/core' and created the AppComponent class with the @Component decorator, selector, and template.
steps.feedbackWrong: import Component from '@angular/core' and create the AppComponent class with basic structure using the @Component decorator.

steps.title: Create a MicroFrontendService with loadModule method
steps.instruction: Create a new Angular service class named MicroFrontendService with a method called loadModule that returns a Promise<string>.
steps.hint: Use the @Injectable decorator and export the class. The loadModule method can return Promise.resolve('Module loaded') for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: A MicroFrontendService class is created with a loadModule method that returns a Promise.
successCriteria: MicroFrontendService class exists with @Injectable decorator and a loadModule method returning Promise<string>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you have both the @Injectable decorator and the loadModule method that returns a Promise<string>.
steps.feedbackWrong: The service wasn't created correctly. Check that you have a class named MicroFrontendService with the @Injectable decorator and a loadModule method.

steps.title: Define MicroFrontend interface for type safety
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript interface named 'MicroFrontend' with two required properties: 'name' of type string and 'url' of type string.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions in curly braces.
steps.expectedOutcome: A TypeScript interface is defined that will be used to type micro-frontend modules.
successCriteria: The MicroFrontend interface is defined with both 'name: string' and 'url: string' properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your interface has both required properties with correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword with proper TypeScript syntax.

steps.title: Initialize available micro-frontends array in AppComponent
steps.instruction: In the AppComponent class, add a property called 'availableMicroFrontends' that is an array of MicroFrontend objects. Initialize it as an empty array.
steps.hint: Define the property with proper TypeScript type annotation: 'availableMicroFrontends: MicroFrontend[] = []'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppComponent now has a typed array property to store micro-frontend definitions.
successCriteria: AppComponent has an 'availableMicroFrontends' property typed as MicroFrontend[] and initialized as an empty array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've defined the property with the correct type annotation 'MicroFrontend[]' and initialized it as an empty array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The availableMicroFrontends property is missing or incorrectly defined. It should be a typed array property in the AppComponent class.

steps.title: Inject MicroFrontendService into AppComponent
steps.instruction: In the AppComponent class, add a constructor that injects the MicroFrontendService as a private dependency.
steps.hint: Use Angular's dependency injection by declaring a constructor parameter with the service type.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: injecting a service into a component
constructor(private userService: UserService) {}
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppComponent constructor will be ready to use the MicroFrontendService for loading modules.
successCriteria: AppComponent has a constructor with a private parameter of type MicroFrontendService.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the constructor parameter is properly typed as MicroFrontendService and marked as private.
steps.feedbackWrong: The constructor injection isn't quite right. Check that you're injecting MicroFrontendService with the correct syntax.

steps.title: Create loadMicroFrontend handler method
steps.instruction: In the AppComponent class, add an async method named loadMicroFrontend that takes a microFrontendId parameter of type string and returns a Promise<void>. Inside the method, call the injected service's loadModule method with the microFrontendId and log the result.
steps.hint: Remember to use the async keyword before the method name and await when calling the service method. The method signature should be: async loadMicroFrontend(microFrontendId: string): Promise<void>
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppComponent now has an async loadMicroFrontend method that will handle loading micro-frontends through the service.
successCriteria: AppComponent contains an async loadMicroFrontend method with correct signature that calls the service's loadModule method.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a method, but check: Is it async? Does it have the correct parameter type? Does it call the service's loadModule method?
steps.feedbackWrong: The loadMicroFrontend method is missing or doesn't match the required signature. Review the async method syntax and service call.

steps.title: Add template structure with container div
steps.instruction: In the AppComponent template, replace the current template with a main container div that will hold the micro-frontend content, and keep the existing heading.
steps.hint: Update the template property in the @Component decorator to include a div element with a class or id for styling and content insertion.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppComponent template now has a container div that will serve as the main area for loading and displaying micro-frontend modules.
successCriteria: The template includes a div element that wraps or follows the heading, providing a structured container for dynamic content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've made progress, but ensure the template includes a div element that can hold the micro-frontend content. Check the structure.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template doesn't yet have the required container div. Review the instruction and try adding a div element in the template.

steps.title: Add micro-frontend selection dropdown
steps.instruction: In the AppComponent template, add a <select> dropdown element with an *ngFor directive to iterate over the availableMicroFrontends array.
steps.hint: Use *ngFor to create an <option> for each micro-frontend in the array, binding its value and display text appropriately.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: dropdown for items array
<select>
  <option *ngFor="let item of items" [value]="item.id">{{ item.name }}</option>
</select>
steps.expectedOutcome: A <select> element appears in the template with options generated from the availableMicroFrontends array.
successCriteria: The template contains a <select> element with an *ngFor directive bound to availableMicroFrontends.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added a <select> element with *ngFor to iterate over availableMicroFrontends.
steps.feedbackWrong: The dropdown isn't properly implemented. Check that you've added a <select> with *ngFor bound to availableMicroFrontends.

steps.title: Add load button and wire to handler
steps.instruction: Add a button element inside the template that triggers the loadMicroFrontend method when clicked.
steps.hint: Use Angular's event binding syntax (click)="loadMicroFrontend()" on a <button> element.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: Button with click handler
<button (click)="handleClick()">Load Content</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Load Micro-Frontend' appears in the UI, and clicking it will call the loadMicroFrontend method.
successCriteria: Button element is present with (click)="loadMicroFrontend()" event binding and appropriate label text.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but it's missing either the click event binding or appropriate label. Make sure to use (click)="loadMicroFrontend()" and include descriptive text.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button element or its event binding is missing. Add a <button> with (click)="loadMicroFrontend()" inside the template.

steps.title: Add status display area
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element below the load button to display loading status messages. Use the template reference variable #status to make it accessible.

successCriteria: A paragraph element with a template reference variable is added to the template below the load button.

steps.feedbackPartial: You added a paragraph, but remember to include a template reference variable (like #status) so it can be accessed from the component.
